title: Louis Armstrong's impact
summary: Armstrong influenced everyone through feeling and economy rather than technique.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Now what about Louie Armstrong? What impact did he have on you, for example, in the recordings you might have heard of him or indeed, have heard him in New York?
Well, when I first heard Armstrong, I

was just as impressed as everyone else was; he was just great, you know? He had a great influence on everybody. I mean, no matter what instrument you were playing, if you were playing what we thought of as jazz or what was called 'jazz' -- you couldn't help but be somewhat influenced by what he did.
And, oh, it's hard to describe my feeling about him, but I guess we're talking about maybe 1925 ...
'24, '25 ... when did he do the "West End Blues"?
Oh, '28 -- or something like that. And what did he do in the early stages -- "Muckles"?
That was a somewhat later tune.
Well, what could I have heard around 1924 or '25?

Well, you wouldn't have heard him solo with King Oliver, but you would have with Henderson and some of the other small group records that he had put out, or maybe it was some of the blues singers that he had recorded with.
Yes, I guess that was it. I don't
remember, you know, the exact year. But I don't know, Jim, exactly.

Without pressing the issue too much, what was it -- I mean, perhaps more specifically, about Armstrong that would have so impressed people? I mean was it ... it wasn't certainly merely just his technical command.

Oh, no -- it was a feeling. It was definitely the feeling. I mean, you can listen to some of the things that he did in those early days where he played very economically. Yeah, he didn't run all over the horn, and you listen to them today, and they sound just as great and they move you just as much as they did then, you know. Maybe even more now, after you've been saturated with these, you know, thousand note-a-bar players.
